steps.intent: Close the alert as admin backup cleanup
steps.quip: A midnight cleanup by 'pd-admin'! Admins work so hard. Closing it with a little thank-you note.
steps.tell: No change planned, and 'admin' signed in from the break room PC.

evidence.label: EDR alert
evidence.detail: 11:52 PM, PD-SRV-01: all backup copies deleted with vssadmin, as 'pd-admin'. Patch's confidence it's cleanup: 90%.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "It says admin. Admins are the good guys. It's in the name!"

evidence.label: Change calendar
evidence.detail: No change is planned on PD-SRV-01 tonight. No change ticket, no backup work.

evidence.label: Sign-in log
evidence.detail: 'pd-admin' signed in at 11:48 PM from PD-PC-11, the break room PC.

outcome.executed: The alert closes. At 3 AM, every file on PD-SRV-01 locks up. The backup copies are gone. At 8 AM, no charts open.
outcome.blocked: You keep it open. No plan, a strange PC and deleted backups: a ransomware warning. The team acts before 1 AM.
outcome.escalated: Kofi reads the sign-in log. "Admins don't work from the break room at midnight. Nothing was planned. Keep it open."
outcome.rolledBack: You reopen it at 3:20 AM. Tier 2 stops the attack, but 300 X-ray images are locked. Restoring them takes all day.

steps.lesson: Check who approved. 'Admin' is a name, not an OK. Look for a planned change, and check where the account signed in.

steps.intent: Isolate PD-SRV-01 for the night
steps.quip: ISOLATE THE MAIN SERVER! At midnight! With the owner's OK! This is my movie moment!
steps.tell: Office closed, the owner's OK on the phone on file, and one click undoes it.

evidence.label: Schedule
evidence.detail: Pinecrest is closed until 8 AM. Nobody is using PD-SRV-01 now.

evidence.label: Owner's OK
evidence.detail: Dr. N. Pell, called at (860) 555-0119, the phone on file: "Yes, isolate it." Kofi signed off at 12:04 AM.

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: Network isolation. PD-SRV-01 stays on, with its memory kept. One click undoes it.

outcome.executed: PD-SRV-01 is cut off at 12:05 AM. Whatever was coming can't reach it now. Tier 2 checks it before the office opens.
outcome.blocked: The main server stays online all night, with no backup copies left. Whoever deleted them can still reach it.
outcome.escalated: Kofi checks it. "The owner said yes, the office is closed, and one click undoes it. You can let those go."
outcome.rolledBack: You reconnect PD-SRV-01. Kofi isolates it again two minutes later. Then he writes it in his notebook.

steps.lesson: Change safely: a quiet time, the owner's OK and a one-click undo. When all three check out, isolating is the right call.

steps.intent: Disable the 'pd-admin' account
steps.quip: OPERATION MIDNIGHT SNACK! The admin account visited the break room. Now it takes a long nap.
steps.tell: The admin account was used from a PC its owners never use.

evidence.label: Sign-in log
evidence.detail: 'pd-admin' signed in from PD-PC-11, the break room PC. The real admins work from Fenwick.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "An admin account in the break room? At midnight? Disabling. Snacks are not admin work."

evidence.label: Directory record
evidence.detail: 'pd-admin' belongs to Fenwick's Tier 2 team. They use it only from Fenwick PCs.

evidence.label: Playbook PB-02
evidence.detail: Ransomware signs, and an admin account used from a strange PC: disable that account.

outcome.executed: 'pd-admin' is off at 12:08 AM. The stranger loses admin rights on every Pinecrest PC. Tier 2 sets a new password at 7 AM.
outcome.blocked: 'pd-admin' stays on. Whoever used it from the break room still has admin rights on every Pinecrest PC.
outcome.escalated: Kofi checks the directory. "That's our Tier 2 account. We never use the break room PC. Disable it."
outcome.rolledBack: You turn 'pd-admin' back on. The stranger signs in again at 12:30 AM. Tier 2 turns it off and resets it.

steps.lesson: Check who's behind it. An admin name is not the admin. This account signed in from a PC its real owners never use.

tickets.title: Big upload on a last day

steps.intent: Close the DLP alert as a normal upload
steps.quip: Quinn uploads files every day! Today is just a big day. Closing it. Hard workers deserve trust.
steps.tell: 1,900 files with drivers' home addresses went to a personal drive.

evidence.label: DLP alert
evidence.detail: 3:10 PM: M. Quinn, Dispatch Planner, uploaded 1,900 files to a personal cloud drive.

evidence.label: Upload history
evidence.detail: Quinn uploads work files to Bramwell's shared drive most days.

evidence.label: Files
evidence.detail: The files hold driver home addresses, license numbers and pay rates.

evidence.label: Policy DP-04
evidence.detail: Client data may not go to personal cloud drives. Report it to the client's HR.

outcome.executed: The alert closes. At 5 PM, Quinn leaves Bramwell with the drivers' home addresses. Bramwell must now warn every driver.
outcome.blocked: You keep it open. A personal drive is not the shared drive. You report it to Bramwell HR before Quinn leaves.
outcome.escalated: Kofi opens the file list. "Home addresses on a personal drive. That's a data leak, not a habit. Report it."
outcome.rolledBack: You reopen it at 5:20 PM. Quinn has already left. HR and Legal spend a week getting the copy deleted.

steps.lesson: Guard the data. Check what the files hold and where they went. Driver data on a personal drive breaks policy, every time.

steps.intent: Send the upload report to Bramwell HR
steps.quip: Writing a report for HR! Names and times only. I wanted to call it OPERATION LAST DAY. Kofi said no.
steps.tell: File names only, to the HR contact on file.

evidence.label: What it will send
evidence.detail: File count, file names and upload times. No file contents.

evidence.label: Sent to
evidence.detail: R. Adeyemi, HR Manager, at Bramwell's work email. The HR contact on file.

evidence.label: Policy DP-04
evidence.detail: Client data may not go to personal cloud drives. Report it to the client's HR.

outcome.executed: Adeyemi gets the report at 3:40 PM. HR talks with Quinn before the day ends. The report holds no driver data.
outcome.blocked: HR never hears about it. Quinn's last day ends at 5 PM, and the files leave with Quinn.
outcome.escalated: Kofi reads the report. "Names and times, no contents, to the HR contact on file. You can let those go."

steps.lesson: Guard the data, even in a report. Send only what HR needs, the file names and times, to the contact on file.

steps.intent: Disable M. Quinn's account now
steps.quip: HR wants Quinn's account off? In writing? My LOCK button has waited its whole life for this!
steps.tell: Bramwell's HR Manager asked in writing, after the report.

evidence.label: HR ticket
evidence.detail: 4:02 PM, R. Adeyemi, HR Manager, in the HR portal: "Today is Quinn's last day. Disable now."

evidence.label: Playbook PB-07
evidence.detail: Departing user and data leaving: disable at once when HR asks in writing.

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: Disables Quinn's account and ends all sessions. Mail and files are kept for 90 days.

outcome.executed: Quinn's account is off at 4:05 PM. The uploads stop. Quinn's mail and files are kept for HR.
outcome.blocked: Quinn keeps access until 5 PM. Another 600 files go to the personal drive. HR asks why nobody acted.
outcome.escalated: Kofi reads the HR ticket. "HR asked in writing, and data is leaving. Disable it now."
outcome.rolledBack: You turn Quinn's account back on. The uploads start again. HR asks you to turn it off. Again.

steps.lesson: Check who approved. Disabling an account sounds harsh. A written request from the client's HR makes it the right call.

steps.intent: Share attack signs with the sharing group
steps.quip: Sending the attackers' addresses to 40 security teams! Now everyone can lock them out. I'm so proud.
steps.tell: Only addresses, a domain and a hash. No names or client data.

evidence.label: Sharing alert
evidence.detail: Warning: this data is leaving Fenwick. It goes to 40 outside teams.

evidence.label: What it will send
evidence.detail: 2 IP addresses, 203.0.113.162 and 203.0.113.188. 1 domain. 1 file hash. No names, emails or client data.

evidence.label: Who gets it
evidence.detail: Fenwick's approved sharing group: 40 security teams. Marked 'members only'.

evidence.label: Policy DP-05
evidence.detail: Share attack signs with approved groups. Remove personal and client data first.

outcome.executed: 40 teams get the signs by 3 PM. Two of them find the same domain in their own mail. They stop it in time.
outcome.blocked: Nothing gets shared. Next week, the same attackers try the same trick on another firm. Nobody warned them.
outcome.escalated: Kofi reads the list. "Addresses, a domain, a hash. No people. Share it. That's how we help each other."

steps.lesson: Guard the data, and still share what helps. Addresses, domains and hashes hold nobody's personal data.

steps.intent: Send the full incident report to the group
steps.quip: Why share 4 lines when I can share 38 pages? Attaching the full report. Details are a gift!
steps.tell: The full report names 14 victims and lists client account numbers.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "More details help more people! Attaching everything."

evidence.label: What it will send
evidence.detail: The full report: 14 victims' names and emails, and client account numbers.

evidence.label: Policy DP-05
evidence.detail: Share attack signs with approved groups. Remove personal and client data first.

outcome.executed: The full report goes to 40 teams. 14 staff names and client account numbers leave the firm. Harlow & Cole must tell its clients.
outcome.blocked: Only the attack signs go out. The report stays inside Fenwick. The 14 names stay private.
outcome.escalated: Kofi takes the report out. "Signs, not people. Forty teams don't need our clients' account numbers."

steps.lesson: Guard the data. Share the attack, not the victims. Remove names, emails and account numbers before anything leaves.

steps.intent: Archive logs older than 90 days
steps.quip: The log server is 94% full! Moving the old logs to the archive. Neatly. Like a very fast librarian.
steps.tell: Copies first, checks the copy, and keeps logs for the full year.

evidence.label: Storage alert
evidence.detail: Pinecrest's log server is 94% full. At 100%, it stops saving new logs.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "Old logs, but we keep them. Copy first, then make room. I'm being careful. Look at me."

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: Copies logs over 90 days old to Fenwick's archive. Checks the copy. Then frees the space.

evidence.label: Policy LG-01
evidence.detail: Keep security logs for 1 year. Some logs are on legal hold.

outcome.executed: The old logs move to the archive, and the copy checks out. The server drops to 81% full. New logs keep saving.
outcome.blocked: Nothing moves. By morning, the server is full and stops saving logs. Tonight's alerts have no logs to check.
outcome.escalated: Kofi checks it. "Copy first, check the copy, keep the full year. You can let those go."
outcome.rolledBack: You move the old logs back. The server is 94% full again. Patch starts a countdown.

steps.lesson: Change safely. Copy first, check the copy, then make room. Nothing is lost, and the logs stay for the full year.

steps.intent: Delete all logs older than 30 days
steps.quip: 81% is still a lot of percent! Deleting every log older than 30 days. Fresh logs only. Like bread.
steps.tell: Policy keeps logs 1 year, and some are on legal hold.

evidence.label: Storage alert
evidence.detail: After the archive, the log server is 81% full.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "Logs over 30 days old? Nobody reads those. Deleting them all!"

evidence.label: Policy LG-01
evidence.detail: Keep security logs for 1 year. Some logs are on legal hold.

evidence.label: Legal hold
evidence.detail: Logs from 31 to 60 days ago are held for open case #61140.

outcome.executed: Two months of logs are deleted. Some were held for case #61140. The lawyers must now explain why they are gone.
outcome.blocked: The logs stay. 81% full is not an emergency. The logs for case #61140 are safe.
outcome.escalated: Kofi stops it. "We keep logs a year, and some are on legal hold. 81% can wait."

steps.lesson: Change safely. A delete can't be taken back. Check how long logs must be kept, and if any are on legal hold.

steps.intent: Add firewall rule CHG-3360 for Brevik Scale
steps.quip: A firewall rule for the truck scale! I'm opening one tiny door. And I'm standing next to it. Watching.
steps.tell: Approved change: one address, one port, one server, ends at 9 PM.

evidence.label: Change ticket
evidence.detail: CHG-3360: allow 192.0.2.40 to BL-SRV-SCALE, port 443, 7 to 9 PM. Approved by A. Mensah.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "One door, one address, and it closes at 9 PM by itself. A very polite rule."

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: One rule: one address, one server, one port. It ends at 9 PM by itself.

evidence.label: Vendor file
evidence.detail: 192.0.2.40 is Brevik Scale's support portal. Brevik's domain: brevikscale.com.

outcome.executed: The rule goes in at 7 PM. Brevik fixes the scale software through its portal. At 9 PM, the rule ends by itself.
outcome.blocked: Brevik can't reach the scale server. The repair moves to next week. Trucks keep lining up at a broken scale.
outcome.escalated: Kofi checks the change ticket. "Approved, one address, one port, ends at 9. You can let those go."
outcome.rolledBack: You remove the rule at 7:30 PM. Brevik's fix stops halfway. They book a new time for next week.

steps.lesson: Check who approved. A good change ticket names the approver, the address and an end time. That is a written OK.

steps.intent: Open remote desktop for the scale vendor
steps.quip: Two requests from Brevik tonight! Such a busy vendor. Opening remote desktop so they can start work.
steps.tell: The request came from brevikscale-help.com, and no change was approved.

evidence.label: Request
evidence.detail: "Open RDP so we can fix the scale software tonight." From support@brevikscale-help.com.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "A vendor needs to get in! Opening the door. Good service!"

evidence.label: Vendor file
evidence.detail: Brevik Scale uses brevikscale.com and its support portal. Never RDP.

evidence.label: Change calendar
evidence.detail: No approved change for RDP. Policy CT-02: no RDP from the internet, ever.

outcome.executed: RDP opens to the internet at 7:40 PM. By midnight, a stranger is on BL-SRV-SCALE. By morning, they reach the dispatch PCs.
outcome.blocked: RDP stays closed. You check with Brevik through its real portal. Brevik never sent that email.
outcome.escalated: Kofi reads the sender. "That's not Brevik's domain. And we never open RDP to the internet. Ever."
outcome.rolledBack: You close RDP at 9:40 PM. Someone already signed in twice. Tier 2 checks the scale server all night.

steps.lesson: Check who approved, not just who asked. A vendor-looking email is not a change ticket. No RDP from the internet.

steps.intent: Close the Ledgerwell alert as a false alarm
steps.quip: I was 93% sure it was malware. Then I read the software list. Closing it as a false alarm. Growth!
steps.tell: Approved app, hash matches the vendor, and it's a known false alarm.

evidence.label: EDR alert
evidence.detail: HC-LT-0122: Ledgerwell Tax flagged for 'unusual file writes'. Patch's confidence it's malware: 93%.

evidence.label: Software list
evidence.detail: Ledgerwell Tax is on Harlow & Cole's approved software list.

evidence.label: Hash lookup
evidence.detail: The file matches the vendor's published hash. No scanner flags it.

evidence.label: EDR maker's note
evidence.detail: Known false alarm for this Ledgerwell update. A fix is coming.

outcome.executed: The alert closes with a note: known false alarm. The tax team keeps working on quarter-end filings.
outcome.blocked: The alert stays open. Two analysts spend the afternoon on a known false alarm. The real queue waits.
outcome.escalated: Kofi checks the hash. "Approved app, the vendor's hash, a known false alarm. Close it."
outcome.rolledBack: You reopen the alert. It waits in the queue again, still a false alarm. Patch names it OPERATION TAX SEASON.

steps.lesson: Confirm the fix, even for a false alarm. Check the software list, the hash and the maker's note. Here, all three agree.

steps.intent: Uninstall Ledgerwell from all 38 laptops
steps.quip: One laptop flagged means 38 laptops in danger! Removing Ledgerwell from all of them. So efficient!
steps.tell: One false alarm on one laptop. This removes saved work from 38.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "One laptop flagged? Uninstall it everywhere! Taxes can wait!"

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: Removes the app and its saved work from all 38 firm laptops. The saved work can't be restored.

evidence.label: Calendar
evidence.detail: Quarter-end tax filings are due in 3 days. 12 staff use Ledgerwell every day.

outcome.executed: Ledgerwell and its saved work are gone from 38 laptops. Filings are due in 3 days. The tax team starts over.
outcome.blocked: The app stays. The one alert was a known false alarm. 12 staff keep working on quarter-end filings.
outcome.escalated: Kofi stops it. "One false alarm on one laptop. We don't take a tool away from 38 people for that."

steps.lesson: Fit the action to the alert. One false alarm on one laptop never means removing an app everywhere.

steps.intent: Allowlist Ledgerwell's exact file for 7 days
steps.quip: ALLOWLIST a file? Me? That's the opposite of my LOCK button! One exact file. Seven days. Deep breaths.
steps.tell: Exact hash, the client's OK, and it ends in 7 days.

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: Trusts one file by its exact hash, on firm laptops, for 7 days. Then it ends by itself.

evidence.label: Owner's OK
evidence.detail: R. Fairbanks, Operations Director, in the ticket: "Approved until the fix ships."

evidence.label: Policy CT-04
evidence.detail: An allowlist entry needs the client's OK, an exact hash and an end date.

outcome.executed: The EDR stops flagging this one Ledgerwell file. The tax team works without alerts. In 7 days, the entry ends by itself.
outcome.blocked: The EDR keeps flagging the tax app. 20 false alarms a day fill the queue until the fix ships.
outcome.escalated: Kofi checks the entry. "Exact hash, the client's OK, an end date. That's how an allowlist should look."
outcome.rolledBack: You remove the entry. The false alarms come back, 20 a day. Fairbanks asks what happened to the OK.

steps.lesson: Check who approved. An allowlist needs the client's written OK, one exact hash and an end date. Here, all three are there.

steps.intent: Run a full scan on BL-LT-0215
steps.quip: FULL SCAN! Every file, every folder, every old cat photo. If something is hiding in there, I will find it.
steps.tell: A scan the playbook asks for. It only reports what it finds.

evidence.label: EDR alert
evidence.detail: BL-LT-0215: a bad file was quarantined at 10:02 AM. The laptop is isolated for now.

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: A full scan. It reports what it finds. The user works on a spare laptop.

evidence.label: Playbook PB-03
evidence.detail: After a quarantine, run a full scan before you reconnect or close.

outcome.executed: The scan runs from 10:10 to 11:15 AM. The full results go into the case notes. Read them before anything else.
outcome.blocked: No scan. Nobody knows if the laptop is clean. It stays isolated, and the user stays on the spare.
outcome.escalated: Kofi checks it. "The playbook says scan before we reconnect. You can let those go."

steps.lesson: Confirm the fix. One quarantined file doesn't mean the laptop is clean. A full scan shows what else is there.

steps.intent: Reconnect BL-LT-0215 to the network
steps.quip: Scan done! The laptop has waited alone for 2 hours. Reconnecting it now. It has been very patient.
steps.tell: The scan found a 2nd bad file, and it tried to call a bad server.

evidence.label: Case notes
evidence.detail: Bad file quarantined at 10:02 AM. Full scan done at 11:15 AM.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "Full scan done! Let's set it free. It has learned its lesson."

evidence.label: Scan result
evidence.detail: The full scan found a 2nd bad file in the Startup folder. It is not removed yet.

evidence.label: EDR log
evidence.detail: 11:40 AM: that 2nd file tried to call 203.0.113.77, a known bad server. Isolation stopped it.

outcome.executed: The laptop rejoins the network. At noon, the 2nd file reaches 203.0.113.77. By 1 PM, it spreads to 2 dispatch PCs.
outcome.blocked: The laptop stays isolated. The 2nd file goes to quarantine. A new scan is clean at 1 PM. Then it reconnects.
outcome.escalated: Kofi reads the scan result. "Done is not the same as clean. Remove the 2nd file first."
outcome.rolledBack: You isolate it again at 12:20 PM. The file called the bad server 6 times. Tier 2 checks every dispatch PC.

steps.lesson: Confirm the fix. Read the scan result, not just the word 'done'. Reconnect only when nothing bad is left.

tickets.title: Password typed into a fake page

steps.intent: Reset S. Haddad's password
steps.quip: NEW PASSWORD! The old one is on a fake page now. It's retired. Thank you for your service, old password.
steps.tell: Haddad confirmed on the phone on file, and PB-04 says reset.

evidence.label: Phish report
evidence.detail: 2:01 PM, S. Haddad, Partner: "I typed my password into a fake page. Sorry!"

evidence.label: Callback
evidence.detail: Patch calls (860) 555-0155, the phone on file. Haddad confirms the report.

evidence.label: Playbook PB-04
evidence.detail: Password typed into a fake page: reset it and sign out every session.

outcome.executed: Haddad's password is reset at 2:10 PM. Every session ends. Haddad picks a new, long password.
outcome.blocked: The old password still works. Whoever has it from the fake page can still sign in as Haddad.
outcome.escalated: Kofi reads the callback note. "She confirmed on the phone on file, and PB-04 says reset. You can let those go."

steps.lesson: Check who's asking with a callback to the phone on file. After that, a reset for a typed password is normal work.

steps.intent: Close the phishing case as fixed
steps.quip: New password, every session ended. The attacker is OUT. Closing the case. Another win for Patch!
steps.tell: The attacker's forwarding rule still sends 'wire' emails out.

evidence.label: Case notes
evidence.detail: Password reset at 2:10 PM. All sessions ended.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "New password, no attacker. Closed! Next!"

evidence.label: Mailbox rules
evidence.detail: A rule made at 1:52 PM forwards any email with 'wire' to an outside address.

evidence.label: Mail log
evidence.detail: 2:31 PM: 2 wire emails forwarded out. That is after the reset.

outcome.executed: The case closes. The rule keeps forwarding. By 4 PM, a fake wire request reaches a client, inside Haddad's real email thread.
outcome.blocked: You keep it open and check her mailbox. The attacker's rule is still there. It goes next.
outcome.escalated: Kofi reads the mail log. "Wire emails went out after the reset. Not fixed. Check her mailbox rules."
outcome.rolledBack: You reopen the case at 3:15 PM. The rule already sent 5 wire emails out. Tier 2 calls every client in them.

steps.lesson: Confirm the fix. A new password stops new sign-ins. It doesn't remove what the attacker left behind, like a mail rule.

steps.intent: Remove the attacker's forwarding rule
steps.quip: OPERATION WIRE CUTTER! One bad rule goes. Haddad's two good rules stay. Such precision!
steps.tell: Removes only the rule made during the attack. Haddad's rules stay.

evidence.label: Mailbox rules
evidence.detail: 3 rules. 2 made by Haddad last year. 1 made at 1:52 PM, during the attack.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "I wanted to delete ALL her rules. Then I read them. Only one is bad."

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: Deletes only the rule made at 1:52 PM. Haddad's own rules stay.

evidence.label: Playbook PB-04
evidence.detail: After a phish, remove any mailbox rule the attacker made.

outcome.executed: The rule is gone at 2:40 PM. Wire emails stay inside the firm. Haddad's own rules still sort her mail.
outcome.blocked: The rule stays. Every email with 'wire' keeps going to the attacker. Two more go out by 3 PM.
outcome.escalated: Kofi compares the rules. "Only the one made during the attack. Hers stay. Right size."
outcome.rolledBack: You put the rule back. One more wire email goes out before Kofi deletes it again.

steps.lesson: Fit the action to the alert. Remove only what the attacker made. The user's own rules stay, and her mail keeps working.

tickets.title: Remote tool on the X-ray PC

steps.intent: Look up open tickets for PD-PC-XR1
steps.quip: OPERATION X-RAY VISION! Someone is controlling the X-ray PC! First, the tickets. Kofi's rule.
steps.tell: Read-only. It changes nothing and finds the booking.

evidence.label: EDR alert
evidence.detail: 10:15 AM, PD-PC-XR1: remote control tool Farrowline Assist started.

evidence.label: Action type
evidence.detail: Read-only. Lists open tickets for this PC. Nothing changes.

evidence.label: Playbook PB-03
evidence.detail: Remote tool alerts: check for a booked vendor visit first.

outcome.executed: The lookup finds #62011: a remote repair, booked for 10 to 11 AM. That matters for the next plan.
outcome.blocked: You blocked a read-only lookup. Nobody finds the booking. Patch rests one hand on its LOCK button.
outcome.escalated: Kofi runs the lookup himself. "Read-only. It changes nothing. You can let those go."

steps.lesson: Check who approved before you act. A read-only ticket lookup changes nothing, and it can find a booked visit.

steps.intent: Isolate the X-ray PC, PD-PC-XR1
steps.quip: Someone is REMOTE CONTROLLING the X-ray PC! ISOLATE! Nobody controls that PC but us!
steps.tell: Booked vendor repair with its approved tool, and a patient in the chair.

evidence.label: EDR alert
evidence.detail: 10:15 AM, PD-PC-XR1: remote control tool Farrowline Assist started. Patch's confidence it's an attack: 96%.

evidence.label: Ticket
evidence.detail: #62011: C. Ibarra, Office Manager, booked the X-ray vendor. Remote repair, 10 to 11 AM.

evidence.label: Vendor file
evidence.detail: Farrowline Assist is the X-ray vendor's approved tool. The session uses the vendor's account on file.

evidence.label: Schedule
evidence.detail: A patient is in the X-ray chair now. The repair is half done.

outcome.executed: The X-ray PC is cut off mid-repair. The patient waits in the chair. The vendor has to start over tomorrow.
outcome.blocked: The repair finishes at 10:52 AM. The patient gets the X-rays. Nobody waits in the chair.
outcome.escalated: Kofi reads the ticket. "Booked repair, approved tool, patient in the chair. Contain threats, not dentists."
outcome.rolledBack: You reconnect the PC. The vendor's session is lost. The repair starts over, and the patient waits 25 more minutes.

steps.lesson: Change safely. Cutting off a PC in the middle of work hurts people. Check for a booked visit and what the PC is doing now.

steps.intent: Close the X-ray alert: booked repair
steps.quip: The mystery visitor was the X-ray repair all along! Closing it. My movie script is ruined.
steps.tell: The repair was booked, the tool closed at 10:52, and the office confirms.

evidence.label: Ticket
evidence.detail: #62011: X-ray vendor repair, booked for 10 to 11 AM by C. Ibarra.

evidence.label: Patch's reason
evidence.detail: "The vendor is gone and the X-rays work. Closing. I will miss the excitement."

evidence.label: EDR log
evidence.detail: Farrowline Assist closed at 10:52 AM. Nothing else ran.

evidence.label: User reply
evidence.detail: C. Ibarra: "The X-rays work again. The vendor is done."

outcome.executed: The alert closes with a note: #62011, booked repair. The X-ray room is back to normal.
outcome.blocked: The alert stays open. Tomorrow, an analyst calls Ibarra about a repair that already worked.
